conceptTag: Handle objections at a software renewal
readerTitle: Two renewal emails: 'too expensive' and 'we're looking elsewhere'
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스 업체의 일정 관리 소프트웨어 갱신, 보험사 고객지원팀의 헬프데스크 소프트웨어 갱신) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 갱신 때 나오는 반론은 거절이 아니라 질문이다. 먼저 고객이 무엇과 비교하는지, 누가 왜 비교하는지 묻고 나서 답한다.
misconception: 갱신 때 '비싸다'거나 '경쟁사를 본다'는 말이 나오면 바로 할인하거나 경쟁사 약점을 짚어야 고객을 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: 영업 실무의 일반 원칙 (가격 반론과 경쟁사 반론 다루기). 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 SAL-03-01, SAL-03-03 참고
모든 인물, 업체, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 놓친 작업 계산: 월 2~3건 × 건당 $120 = $240~$360. 월 요금 $180보다 큼. 2건만 막아도 $240 > $180. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
알림 문자가 노쇼를 '모두' 막는다고 단정하지 않도록 카드에 'can help prevent'와 'can't promise'로 적었습니다. 실제 효과 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.
SAL-03-01, SAL-03-03 개념 레슨의 실제 내용(정의, 표현)과 이 레슨의 요약 문장이 일치하는지 게시 전에 확인하세요.

cards.title: Two renewal emails: 'too expensive' and 'we're looking elsewhere'
body: You sell software on yearly plans. A few weeks before each renewal, the same two emails show up.
*"It's too expensive."* *"We're looking at another tool."* Neither one is a no yet. Today you'll handle both, using two ideas from this unit.

image.label: Two emails on a laptop screen with a renewal date circled
image.brief: 노트북 화면에 이메일 두 통. 하나는 제목 "Too expensive", 다른 하나는 "Looking at another tool". 옆 달력에 갱신일이 빨간 동그라미로 표시됨. 실제 메일 서비스나 회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Dana wants to go back to a spreadsheet.
body: Dana runs a home cleaning company with 12 cleaners. She pays you $180 a month for scheduling software. At renewal she writes: "Honestly, it's too expensive for what we use. I can manage with a spreadsheet."

options.text: Offer 20% off if she renews this week
options.feedback: It might keep the account, but it confirms the price was the problem and teaches her that pushing back pays. You still don't know why $180 felt high.

options.text: Ask what she uses it for each week and what the spreadsheet would cost her
options.feedback: This handles it as a **price objection**: price feels high when value is hidden. Asking first shows what she's comparing $180 against.

options.text: Send her a list of the new features added this year
options.feedback: It shows effort, but features she doesn't use won't make $180 feel smaller. You're answering before you know the question.

cards.title: She was using one feature.
body: Dana uses the app for one thing: the weekly schedule. She never switched on the automatic reminder texts to clients.
Almost in passing, she mentions that two or three clients a month aren't home when the cleaner arrives. Each missed job is about $120 she doesn't get back.
The price wasn't wrong. She was comparing $180 against a free spreadsheet, not against what the tool could prevent.

cards.title: Put the $180 next to the right thing.

breakdown.label: Monthly price
breakdown.detail: What Dana sees on the invoice

breakdown.label: Spreadsheet
breakdown.detail: Free, but she builds the schedule by hand every week

breakdown.label: Missed jobs
breakdown.detail: 2–3 a month × $120, which reminders can help prevent

cards.callout: You can't promise reminders stop every missed job. But preventing just two a month covers the price.

cards.title: A price objection is usually a value question.
body: From the lesson on price objections: when a customer says "too expensive", first ask *compared to what?* The answer tells you whether to show hidden value, change the plan, or accept it's not a fit.

With Dana, you did the first. You set up the reminders together on the call. If she still felt it was too much, the next move is a **trade, not a discount**: a smaller plan with fewer features, for less money.

cards.title: Now the customer is a team inside a big company.
body: Priya runs a 15-person support team at a regional insurance company. Her team uses your help-desk software every day.
Two months before renewal, someone from purchasing emails: "We're evaluating a competitor that is 30% cheaper." What do you do?

options.text: Send a comparison showing where the competitor falls short
options.feedback: Attacking a rival makes you sound worried and puts the buyer on the defensive. And purchasing may not care about the gaps you list.

options.text: Match the 30% to end the discussion
options.feedback: It may close the renewal, but you give up 30% without knowing whether price is even the reason. Next year the same email comes back.

options.text: Ask purchasing what started the review, and ask Priya what her team would lose by switching
options.feedback: This is the **competitor objection** at work: learn what the comparison is really for before you answer it. Purchasing and Priya may want different things.

cards.title: Find out what the comparison is for.
body: From the lesson on competitor objections: "we're looking at a competitor" can mean a real search, a company rule to collect quotes, or a lever to get a lower price. Each needs a **different answer**.
Here, purchasing had a rule: review every contract above a set size. Priya didn't want to switch. Moving 15 people mid-year meant retraining and losing years of ticket history.
So you helped purchasing build an honest side-by-side, including the cost of switching, for Priya to sign off.

image.label: A buyer and a team manager looking at the same contract from different sides
image.brief: 테이블 양쪽에 두 사람. 왼쪽 구매 담당자는 가격표와 계산기를, 오른쪽 팀장은 팀원 15명 아이콘과 "Ticket history" 폴더를 들고 있음. 가운데에 같은 계약서 한 장. 실제 회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Sometimes the honest answer is 'switch'.
body: These ideas help customers see value clearly. They don't turn every renewal into a win. If Dana truly only needs a schedule, a cheaper plan or even a spreadsheet may be right for her.

If the rival really fits Priya's team better, say so and make leaving easy, with clean data exports. Don't invent deadlines like "this price ends Friday" unless it's true. A customer who leaves well may come back, and will tell others how you behaved.

cards.title: At renewal, ask before you answer.
body: Two ideas did the work today. *Price objections:* ask what the price is compared against, then show hidden value or trade scope instead of discounting. *Competitor objections:* find out what the comparison is for, and who wants it.
**Try it today:** pick one customer renewing in the next 90 days. Write down what they'd compare your price against, and who besides your contact has a say.
